title: Making connections: do we need a model?
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino, a secondary science teacher, asks whether a shared visual model could help students connect ideas within biology and across the sciences. She notes that experts hold a rich mental network of links that novices lack, and that student experience varies with each teacher's expertise. Drawing on Johnstone's triangle from chemistry, Jasper Green's added cellular level, and a published DNA triangle for meiosis, she considers a biology equivalent. She is careful about working memory limits, suggesting such models suit consolidation rather than first introduction, and proposes discussion at department level before adopting anything.
points: Experts see links between topics that novices cannot, so connections should be made explicit rather than left to chance.
Johnstone's triangle (macroscopic, sub-microscopic, symbolic) may be adaptable to biology, though nested biological concepts limit it.
Such models risk overloading working memory if used to introduce concepts, so they fit better after content is learned in chunks.
Standardising how a department makes links protects students from depending on one teacher's expertise.
quotes: To a Biology specialist, like me, making connections between cell structure, the digestive system and aerobic respiration would probably be much easier than it would be for one of my Year 10 students.
As experts in our subjects, we have this mental network in our minds and the more experience we have at teaching our subject, the more robust these connections become.

I think that a framework making explicit a lot of the links between Biological phenomena and theories as well as ideas from the other Sciences would be hugely beneficial to teachers who may not always make those connections. Importantly, it will also be useful to share our thinking with our students.
Essentially, Johnstone’s triangle is a model to represent the macroscopic, sub-microscopic and symbolic levels when teaching Chemistry.

It has become increasingly clear to me that for students to appreciate and apply their knowledge of Science to various concepts, it is important for them to make connections and transfer their knowledge from one aspect to another. Helping our students think of the interconnectedness in Science can come from the way we teach but I would argue it is also important to aim to standardise how we do this. If we do not, then students may only get half the picture depending on who they were taught by, which in turn would depend on the expertise of that teacher.

Another consideration when using triangles or tetrahedrons (with the added microscopic level) is the impact on our students’ working memories (Reid, N., 2009). These devices will not be useful when introducing concepts as there will be just too much to focus on at once.

As with everything else that is introduced, using a framework such as a triangle or a tetrahedron could very easily mutate to have absolutely no impact. Indeed, it could have the opposite effect and add to the cognitive load of our students for no actual gain.
